title: Rahab's scarlet cord (Joshua 2)
hook: a woman on the city wall hides two spies and hangs a red cord from her window

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joshua heard be strong, again and again, and your line was I will not fail you. What first step did you take? Day six hundred ninety-eight.

A red line hangs from a window in a city wall. Behind it, a woman is waiting. A little earlier, Joshua sent two men across the river to spy out Jericho, and in the King James words they "came into an harlot's house, named Rahab, and lodged there." The Bible doesn't tidy up who she is. Her house is built into the town wall itself. Word reaches the king of Jericho that Israelite spies are inside, and his men come to her door. Rahab has already taken the spies up to her roof and hidden them under stalks of flax she had laid out on the roof. She tells the king's men the strangers left at dark, and if they hurry, they'll catch them. Today: why she did it, and what that red line means.
screen: `TWO SPIES, ONE HOUSE IN THE WALL.`

segments.voice: Rahab gives her reason in her own words, and it's a confession from an outsider. She tells the spies her city has heard what Israel's God has done, and their hearts have melted. Then, in the King James Bible: "for the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath." Those words echo, almost exactly, what Moses tells Israel in Deuteronomy. A Canaanite woman, inside a city about to fall, speaks Israel's own creed back to Israel's spies. Then she asks for one thing. The Hebrew word is chesed: loyal kindness. I showed you kindness; show kindness to my father's house. Spare my parents, my brothers, my sisters. The spies agree and give her a sign. She lets them down from her window by a cord, and they tell her: "thou shalt bind this line of scarlet thread in the window which thou didst let us down by." Everyone inside that house will be safe. Then comes the chapter's quiet detail. As soon as the spies are gone: "And she bound the scarlet line in the window." She doesn't wait for the army. She hangs the sign of the promise while nothing has happened yet, and lives under it. Readers have found more than one thing in that thread. Some Christian readers see it as a picture of rescue through blood, like the blood on the doorposts at Passover. Others simply see a woman staking her family on a promise from strangers. And the story doesn't end with Jericho. The letter to the Hebrews names her: "By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace." James praises what she did. Matthew's family line of Jesus includes a Rachab, traditionally taken to be her. The woman on the wall ends up inside the story.
screen: `SHE TIES IT BEFORE THE ARMY COMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help someone at a risk to yourself. Settle, and breathe. Rahab's risk was her life. Yours can be far smaller: speaking up for someone who's being talked about, sitting with the person nobody else sits with, giving time you'd rather keep, saying out loud that you agree with the unpopular one. Let one person come to mind who could use someone on their side. Ask what it would cost you to help, and whether you can pay it today. If you pray, you can hold that person up by name. If you don't, simply keep them in mind and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Rahab's scarlet cord. The red line she tied in her window: the sign of a promise, hung before anyone came to keep it.
Your line: the cord in the window. Today, do the helpful thing you named, even if it costs you a little, and do it before you're sure it's safe. Day six hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Christians meet Rahab in sermons on Hebrews 11 and on welcoming outsiders, and some churches teach the scarlet cord as a sign of rescue.

fork.setup: you're Rahab. the king's men are at your door asking for two Israelite spies, who are hidden on your roof. what do you do?
options: hide them and send the king's men away.
run with them to the Israelite camp.
fork.reveal: she tells the searchers to hurry after men already gone, then asks the spies for kindness to her family. readers still argue about her lie; Hebrews remembers her for her faith.

original.note: Hebrew: loyal kindness. Rahab asks the spies to answer her chesed with chesed (Joshua 2:12).

trapdoor: what you thought: a red rope in a battle story.
what it means: the sign of a promise between an outsider and Israel, tied in the window right away.
what a scholar hears: Rahab asks for chesed for chesed (Joshua 2:12), echoes Deuteronomy 4:39, and Hebrews 11:31 names her for faith.

notes: Joshua 2:11 is said to echo Deuteronomy 4:39 'almost exactly' (KJV Deut 4:39: 'the LORD he is God in heaven above, and upon the earth beneath'). Confirm the wording.
'Some Christian readers' seeing the scarlet line as a picture of rescue through blood: the reading goes back at least to 1 Clement 12; not cited by name in the script. Confirm it is fairly stated.
Matthew 1:5's Rachab is identified with Rahab as 'traditionally taken to be her'; some scholars question the identification. Confirm the hedge.
The fork reveal names Rahab's lie and says readers still wrestle with it; confirm the tone.
Chesed in Joshua 2:12 (כִּי־עָשִׂיתִי עִמָּכֶם חָסֶד). Confirm pointing and pronunciation.

Editor (y3 audit): 'flax laid out to dry' cut to what 2:6 says (laid in order on the roof); fork reveal no longer says Rahab sent the searchers toward the river (2:7 says they chose that way), and 'wrestle' changed to 'argue' so it does not pre-empt day 700.
